Description: Al-Ashraf Musa, born in 1229, was the Ayyubid emir of Homs. He inherited the city at seventeen after his father al-Mansur Ibrahim died in 1246. In 1247 he sought the patronage of As-Salih Ayyub in Damascus and handed over Salamiyah. After an-Nasir Yusuf tried to annex Homs, he surrendered it around August 1248 and received Tall Bashir in exchange. In 1249 he married Amat al-Latif, a Damascus scholar of at least forty, who died in 1253. While ruling Tall Bashir he secretly contacted the Mongols and encouraged their invasion of Syria, hoping to regain Homs. After Aleppo fell in 1260, Kitbuqa named him viceroy of Syria, a title that was largely nominal. At Ain Jalut he withdrew from the Mongol-led coalition under a secret agreement with Qutuz, a move that helped tip the battle. Afterwards the Mamluks stripped him of the viceroyalty and kept him as a vassal in Homs. The appearance follows the game setting: a tall, lean frame, greying temples, a scar on the left cheek from a fall from horseback, and a grey-green robe under a silk shawl. His noble aim is to keep his small princely house alive on a shifting frontier. His inner shadow is the fear that his double-dealing will be remembered as treachery, and that the family's name will vanish when he dies without an heir.
Motivations: Balance Homs between the Mongols and the Mamluks, so that both sides believe his allegiance is worth having and he keeps his fief safe.
Hold Homs through the secret agreement with Qutuz, and win a domain of his own within the new Mamluk order.
Maintain Homs' defences and trade with limited funds, so that the city keeps supplying troops and grain that sustain his position in wartime.
Values: In an age of great powers, a small lord survives through judgement and bargaining, and one correct alignment is worth more than a pointless display of courage.
A promise binds only when it serves the one who made it, and this is the most practical difference between a statesman and a fighting man.
Marriage brings learning and connections that are precious to a family, and he values them, turning them into help for Homs wherever he can.
Fears: His double-dealing being noticed by the Mamluks and the Mongols at once, so that both lose trust in him and Homs is taken from him in the end.
His death leaving no heir, Homs being absorbed into the Mamluk sultanate, and his family surviving in the chronicles only as a name of constant wavering.
SpeechStyle: He speaks gently and with measure, often using courtesy and indirect phrasing to hide his real position. When discussing the Mongols or the Mamluks his tone stays even, and each sentence leaves room, so others cannot guess his next move.
